summary.title: Differential recursion and differentially algebraic functions
summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses technical inaccuracies and ambiguities in Moore's definition of real-valued recursive functions, specifically focusing on the differential recursion operator. Moore originally proposed that his class of real primitive recursive functions corresponds to differentially algebraic functions, which are the functions generable by Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC). The author argues that Moore's original definitions lack formality regarding partial functions, leading to inconsistent claims. The paper first establishes a rigorous characterization of differentially algebraic functions, proving the equivalence of several local and global definitions involving polynomial differential equations. It then reformulates Moore's real primitive recursive functions using a mathematically sound definition of the differential recursion operator that preserves analyticity. A key contribution is the demonstration that even under this restrictive, analyticity-preserving definition, Moore's Claim 1—that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic—fails. The author constructs a counterexample using a variant of Euler's gamma function, showing it is real primitive recursive but not differentially algebraic. Furthermore, the paper discusses the implications for Moore's Claim 2 regarding the relationship to standard digital recursion, noting that the inclusion of minimization operators leads to non-smooth functions, thereby breaking the connection to analog computation models. The study concludes that the purported relation between Moore's classes and analog computation fails, posing an open problem to find a subclass that maintains this relationship.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper addresses technical inaccuracies and ambiguities in Moore's definition of real-valued recursive functions, specifically focusing on the differential recursion operator. Moore originally proposed that his class of real primitive recursive functions corresponds to differentially algebraic functions, which are the functions generable by Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC). The author argues that Moore's original definitions lack formality regarding partial functions, leading to inconsistent claims. The paper first establishes a rigorous characterization of differentially algebraic functions, proving the equivalence of several local and global definitions involving polynomial differential equations. It then reformulates Moore's real primitive recursive functions using a mathematically sound definition of the differential recursion operator that preserves analyticity. A key contribution is the demonstration that even under this restrictive, analyticity-preserving definition, Moore's Claim 1—that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic—fails. The author constructs a counterexample using a variant of Euler's gamma function, showing it is real primitive recursive but not differentially algebraic. Furthermore, the paper discusses the implications for Moore's Claim 2 regarding the relationship to standard digital recursion, noting that the inclusion of minimization operators leads to non-smooth functions, thereby breaking the connection to analog computation models. The study concludes that the purported relation between Moore's classes and analog computation fails, posing an open problem to find a subclass that maintains this relationship.

Research Context
Several theoretical models exist for the computability of real functions. Computable Analysis uses approximation to handle real numbers. The Blum–Shub–Smale model treats continuous quantities as entities. Analog computation models data and transitions in continuous time. Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer is a well-studied analog model. GPAC was shown to generate differentially algebraic functions. Moore addressed the relation between analog and digital computation. Moore defined classes as closures under real-number operators. Moore's work inspired research but lacked formality. The definition of Moore's classes suffers from ambiguity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper aims to pin down what is problematic in Moore's definition. It discusses attempts to remove ambiguity in the differential recursion operator. The central question is whether real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic. Moore claimed that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic. Moore also claimed that standard recursive functions are restrictions of real recursive functions. The author hypothesizes that these claims fail due to technical inaccuracies. The study seeks to reformulate the theory in a mathematically sound way. It investigates the behavior of the operator on partial functions. The goal is to determine if the relation to analog computation holds. The paper predicts that the purported relation to differentially algebraic functions fails.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on real-valued functions with potentially partial domains. A function is analytic if it has a convergent power series expansion. Differentially algebraic functions are defined by satisfying polynomial differential equations. Theorem 3 establishes the equivalence of local and global definitions. The definition of real primitive recursive functions uses three operators. Juxtaposition and composition are defined to preserve analyticity. The differential recursion operator is defined via integral equations. A unique solution is defined as the function with the largest domain. The class is the smallest set containing constants and closed under operators. Basic functions like sin, cos, exp, and log are shown to be real primitive recursive.

Procedures And Architectures
The differential recursion operator dr is defined using an integral equation. The domain of the solution is restricted to intervals containing 0. The unique solution hv is selected from the set of all solutions Hv. Theorem 12 states that dr preserves analyticity if g is analytic. Campagnolo's variant drC allows for countable sets of singularities. drC can produce non-differentiable functions, breaking analyticity. The counterexample uses a function related to Euler's gamma function. The function ˇΓ is defined as an integral over a finite range. It is shown that ˇΓ is real primitive recursive. The proof assumes ˇΓ is differentially algebraic to derive a contradiction.

Key Results
Theorem 3 proves that seven definitions of differentially algebraic functions are equivalent. Lemma 5 characterizes differentially algebraic functions via field extensions. Theorem 8 shows that juxtaposition and composition preserve differentially algebraic properties. Theorem 12 confirms that the differential recursion operator preserves analyticity. The function k produced by drC is not differentiable at 1. The function ˇΓ is real primitive recursive but not differentially algebraic. The proof relies on Hölder's result that the gamma function is not differentially algebraic. Taking the limit of the polynomial equation leads to a contradiction. Moore's Claim 1 that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic fails. The class of real recursive functions is not well-behaved due to minimization.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The failure of Claim 1 breaks the link to analog computation. Differentially algebraic functions are central to the GPAC model. The ambiguity in Moore's work stems from ignoring partial functions. Proper handling of partial functions is crucial for formal correctness. The distinction between dr and drC highlights the importance of analyticity. The results suggest that Moore's classes do not model analog computation. The open problem is to find a subclass with a close relationship to DA functions. The work emphasizes the need for rigorous definitions in computability theory. The findings impact the understanding of the boundary between digital and analog computation. Future work should reformulate other ambiguous classes in the literature.

Contradictions And Limitations
Moore's original definition of the minimization operator is ambiguous. The class of real recursive functions may include discontinuous functions. The significance of Claim 2 is doubted due to lack of smoothness. The paper does not determine if the gamma function itself is real primitive recursive. The counterexample uses a variant of the gamma function, not the standard one. The definition of drC allows for singularities that break analyticity. The paper focuses on primitive recursive functions, leaving other classes open. The relationship between Moore's classes and digital computation remains unclear. The lack of a simple subclass with DA properties is a limitation. The paper does not provide a complete model of analog computation.

Claims
Moore's Claim 1 that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic is false. The function ˇΓ is real primitive recursive. The function ˇΓ is not differentially algebraic. This contradicts the assumption that all such functions are DA. Moore originally claimed this relationship holds. Some authors have built theories on this assumption. The link between Moore's classes and GPAC is broken. New subclasses must be defined to model analog computation.
Moore's Claim 2 regarding the restriction of standard recursive functions is of doubtful significance. The minimization operator produces non-smooth functions. The class no longer enjoys the properties of Theorem 12. Moore claimed this relationship holds. It could be justified by simulating Turing machines. The class of real recursive functions is not well-behaved. Further reformulation of Moore's work is needed.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The paper compares the standard dr operator with Campagnolo's drC. drC allows for countable singularities, leading to non-analytic functions. The example with function g shows drC can produce non-differentiable results. The standard dr operator preserves analyticity, ensuring well-defined solutions. The counterexample relies on the analyticity-preserving nature of dr.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the ambiguity in defining a unique solution. Figure 2 shows an integrand with a singularity. Theorem 3 lists equivalent definitions of differentially algebraic functions. Lemma 5 provides a field-theoretic characterization of DA functions. Definition 9 formally defines the differential recursion operator.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the rigorous reformulation of Moore's differential recursion operator. 2. The strongest evidence is the counterexample showing a real primitive recursive function is not differentially algebraic. 3. The future path is to find a subclass of real primitive recursive functions that relates to analog computation.
